answers.answer: The producer publishes the export job ID and render inputs. After the broker confirms acceptance under its durability rules, the API can truthfully return accepted with the job ID. The broker holds the job for a worker. The worker renders and saves the file and ready status, then acknowledges processing so that delivery can be retired. The file is ready only after the required result has been saved; broker acceptance alone is not completion. Users check pending, ready or failed status, and must see failed if processing ultimately fails. A login decision must remain synchronous because granting access depends on its final result; an unresolved queued decision cannot authorize access. Operating the broker and workers is an added cost.

evidence.quote: The API publishes a message containing the job ID and receipt inputs. It confirms the handoff before telling the client the job was accepted.
Holds work for consumers. A publisher confirmation means broker acceptance under the configured durability rules, not a completed receipt.
Receives the message, saves the receipt and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker. A consumer acknowledgement lets the broker retire that delivery.
The client checks that ID for pending, ready, or failed status. Only ready means the receipt can be used; an accepted response is not the receipt.
Authorization must finish before showing a private receipt. Queueing the decision and granting access immediately would use a result we do not yet have.
The tradeoff includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog. A queue does not solve sustained overload.

answers.answer: With at-least-once delivery, the broker may deliver the credit job again because the acknowledgement was not received. Acknowledging before the credit risks retiring the delivery and then crashing before the balance changes, losing the work. Give the business credit operation one stable ID reused on every attempt. In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table protected by a unique constraint and apply the balance credit. Commit both or neither. On a duplicate ID skip the credit. A separate duplicate check followed by a credit is unsafe because attempts can race or crash between them. This makes these database effects duplicate-safe; it does not establish universal exactly-once message delivery or atomic external effects.

evidence.quote: A worker commits its database changes, then crashes before acknowledging. With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again. Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Repeating the same operation has the same effect as doing it once. Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.

In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the receipt changes. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect. A separate check followed by a write can race or crash between steps.
That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

answers.answer: Retry the temporarily inaccessible image store with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget, since immediate repeated retries can worsen an outage. If that budget is exhausted, isolate the job in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status. The unsupported format will not recover simply by waiting, so isolate it rather than repeatedly retrying it. Isolating failed jobs lets healthy jobs continue. Before deliberate replay, fix the cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect; replay must still be duplicate-safe. The dead-letter queue contains the failure but does not repair it.

evidence.quote: A temporary storage outage may recover. Retry with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries can deepen the outage.
An unsupported receipt format will not improve with waiting. Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Healthy jobs can continue. Before deliberately replaying a failed job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. Replay still needs duplicate safety.
A dead-letter queue contains failure; it does not repair the job.

answers.answer: The final quantity could incorrectly be 5: the later event writes 2 first, then the slower earlier event overwrites it with 5. Receiving jobs in order does not guarantee their effects finish in order. Serialize effects by item ID, keeping the later update waiting while the earlier update runs or retries. Different item IDs can execute concurrently. If the earlier update is isolated in a dead-letter queue, repair or cancel that dependency before releasing dependent updates. For a busy item, this serialization creates a throughput bottleneck.

evidence.quote: Two updates change one receipt's address: old, then new. Workers receive them in order, but the slower old update finishes last and overwrites new.
Serialize effects per receipt ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different receipts can still run in parallel. A busy receipt becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.
Ordered delivery alone does not guarantee ordered effects.

answers.answer: Backlog grows by approximately 120 minus 80 = 40 jobs per second while those rates persist. Growing oldest-job age signals increasing waiting time and a risk of violating the promised delay. Bound worker concurrency at the image store safe limit; adding concurrency to a saturated dependency risks more contention. Apply producer backpressure by throttling or rejecting new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer only within an agreed limit. Queue storage and retention are finite: buffering absorbs a burst only if capacity subsequently catches up before storage, retention or allowed-delay limits are reached. More workers help when the workers are the bottleneck and the downstream image store has spare capacity, which it currently does not.

evidence.quote: If 100 receipt jobs arrive each second and 70 finish, unfinished work grows by 30 jobs per second. Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.
Storage and retention are finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached.
Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity. If the database is already saturated, more workers increase contention instead.

answers.answer: One work queue with competing billing and analytics workers distributes jobs between those workers; it does not independently give every event to both applications, and failures can cause repeat deliveries. A retained log can give billing its own consumer group and analytics another, so each application independently processes the purchase events. Each group tracks its own offset for each partition, while workers within that group share the partitions. Committing an offset records progress without deleting retained records. Analytics can rewind its offsets and replay a day only if all required events remain under the retention policy when it replays them. Adding partitions or consumers does not create global ordering, because ordering is per partition. Retention and offsets also do not make external effects exactly once: recording broker progress is not atomic with arbitrary business effects.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides receipt jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.

If receipts and analytics each need every purchase event, a retained log such as Kafka supports separate consumer groups. A partition is an ordered slice of the log. Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions.
Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event. Analytics can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy.
Ordering is per partition, not global across all partitions. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
These acknowledgements cover different boundaries. Neither makes a broker operation atomic with a database write or proves an arbitrary business effect succeeded.
